steps.title: D9 - Q1 — Why the nested chain is harder to reason about
steps.narration: Two concrete reasons, both visible in the T1/T2 diff. First, indentation tracks nothing meaningful in the nested version — six levels deep by the time you reach the actual render call, purely because that's how many .then()s came before it, not because the logic itself is six layers of complexity. The async/await version stays at one indent level for the whole sequential story. Second, each .then() callback is a brand-new anonymous function with its own closure scope, so following one value (like caseJson) across the chain means tracking which nested scope you're in and whether each level correctly `return`s its inner promise to the next .then(). Miss a return and the chain silently breaks — which is exactly the historical loadEvidenceData bug in this same file (Demo 3/5): a missing return meant its caller had no way to know when — or whether — the fetch had actually finished. await reads like ordinary synchronous assignment, so there's no return-to-pass-it-on convention to forget. Both versions run identically — this is a pure readability difference, not a behavioral one (see Q5).

steps.title: D9 - Q2 — What `await` actually does to execution
steps.narration: await pauses execution of only the async function it's inside, at that exact line, until the awaited Promise settles — but it does NOT block the JS engine's single thread. Execution unwinds back out of the async function to whatever called it, exactly as if the function had reached the end of its synchronous portion; the rest of the program — other event handlers, timers, rendering, unrelated Promises — keeps running normally the whole time. Once the awaited Promise settles, the function's remaining body is scheduled to resume as a microtask. The debugger trace from T4 shows the very start of this directly: at the first await (before it had even settled), the sync call stack still showed loadCorePeopleAndLocations <- loadAllData <- initApp with nothing extra queued — because at that exact instant nothing had suspended yet; the suspend/resume only becomes observable once that first await's Promise actually settles and hands control back to just this function's continuation.

steps.title: D9 - Q3 — An `async` function always returns a Promise
steps.narration: Proven live in the running app (Playwright browser_evaluate against the real page): imported js/dataLoading.js and called the real refactored loadAllData(). `loadAllData() instanceof Promise` -> true. Calling `.then(v => v)` on it and logging the resolved value gave `undefined` — because loadAllData()'s body has no explicit return statement, so its implicit return value is undefined, but it's still genuinely wrapped in a real Promise object, not handed back directly. To prove the other half unambiguously — that even an explicit `return someValue` for a plain value still gets Promise-wrapped — also ran an isolated snippet in the same page: `async function demoReturnsPlainValue() { return 42; }` -> instanceof Promise -> true, and `.then(v => v)` resolved to 42, not a synchronously-returned 42. You always have to unwrap it.

steps.title: D9 - Q4 — The `async`/`await` equivalent of `.catch()`
steps.narration: try { await somePromise; } catch (err) { ... } — exactly what got applied to loadEvidenceData() in T3. Verified live what happens if you forget it: defined an async function that awaits a Promise.reject(...), and called it WITHOUT await or a try/catch around the call — the genuine "forgot the catch" scenario. Captured a real window unhandledrejection event firing with the actual error's message, and the browser's own console logged a real "Uncaught (in promise) Error" with a full stack trace. So the rejection doesn't vanish and doesn't crash the script either — it surfaces as an unhandled Promise rejection, the same class of signal a thrown error in a .then() chain with no .catch() would produce, just reported through the unhandledrejection event / console instead of stopping execution at the await site (the awaiting function has already suspended and control has moved on by the time it fires).

steps.title: D9 - Q5 — Is `async`/`await` faster than `.then()`? No.
steps.narration: No — and the T4 debugger trace is direct proof: the actual sequence of operations (fetch case, parse case, assign, fetch people, parse people, assign, fetch locations, parse locations, assign, render) is identical, in the identical order, to what the nested .then() chain did. async/await is syntax sugar over the same Promise machinery — the engine still suspends the function at each await and resumes it as a microtask once the underlying Promise settles, the exact mechanism .then() uses underneath. Nothing changes about the number of requests, their relative timing, or total wall-clock time — this refactor is purely about how the same execution is written and read, not how it executes. Actually making it faster would mean changing WHAT gets awaited and WHEN — e.g. Promise.all to run independent fetches concurrently — which stays deliberately out of scope here per the Task 2 instruction to preserve sequential behavior exactly.

steps.title: D9 - Q6 — Deliberately breaking the refactor by dropping an `await`
steps.narration: Temporarily changed `const caseJson = await caseRes.json();` to `const caseJson = caseRes.json();` — dropped the await, function still async — reloaded the real app, and confirmed live: state.caseData held an actual Promise object (Object.prototype.toString -> "[object Promise]"), not the parsed case data. Real, visible breakage followed: the Dashboard's case header fell back to its default placeholder "Case" instead of "Project ReMotion – Investigation Portal", and the status badge showed "UNKNOWN" instead of "OPEN" — because dashboard.js reads caseData.title/.status off what's actually a pending Promise, and that property access just silently returns undefined, which the render code falls back on. Restored the await immediately after and reconfirmed the fix (title and OPEN both back). This is precisely the same bug category as the Demo 3/5 loadEvidenceData issue in this very file: a Promise read as if it were already the resolved value — there a missing `return` silently discarded a Promise's completion signal, here a missing `await` left a Promise object sitting where real data was expected. Same root mistake, opposite syntax.

steps.title: D10 - T1 (1/2) — `certaintyBadgeClass` to an arrow function
steps.narration: First arrow-function conversion: certaintyBadgeClass in timeline.js. It's a pure module-private lookup — no this, no arguments, never used as a constructor — called only from renderTimeline in the same file, so it's a clean candidate. Converted from a function declaration to a const arrow function. Behaviorally identical: verified live after the change by reloading the Timeline view and confirming all 15 rendered events still carry the correct badge class per certainty (confirmed to reviewed, contradictory to critical, reported to flagged, everything else to unreviewed).

steps.title: D10 - T1 (2/2) — `statCardHTML` to an arrow function
steps.narration: Second good candidate: statCardHTML in dashboard.js, a pure template-string helper called five times from renderDashboard to build the stat-card row. Same reasoning as certaintyBadgeClass — no this/arguments/constructor use, module-private, only called at runtime after the module has fully evaluated. Verified live: reloaded the Dashboard and confirmed all five stat cards (18 Evidence items, 6 People, 6 Locations, 0 Bookmarked, 1 Reviewed) still render with the same markup and values as before the conversion.

steps.title: D10 - T2 — anonymous `addEventListener` callback to an arrow function
steps.narration: The required addEventListener conversion: the hypConfidence range slider's input listener in main.js, previously an anonymous function(e) {...}. It only reads e.target.value and writes it into the confidence-value output — no this, nothing that needs a fresh binding per call. Converted to an arrow function. Verified live: set the slider's value to 77 and dispatched a real input event — hypConfidenceValue's text updated to "77", identical to the pre-conversion behavior.

steps.title: D10 - T3 — deliberately NOT converted: `handleEvidenceListClick`
steps.narration: The one function I deliberately left as a function declaration: handleEvidenceListClick in evidence.js. It's registered directly by reference — container.addEventListener("click", handleEvidenceListClick), not wrapped in another callback — implementing click-delegation over the evidence card list. A function attached this way is called by the DOM with this bound to the listening element (container), which is the actual contract of the delegated-click pattern here. This version reads event.target rather than this, but converting it to an arrow function would permanently and silently discard that binding, since an arrow function always captures this from its enclosing module scope (undefined, strict mode) instead of whatever the caller supplies — foreclosing a very standard DOM pattern for anyone maintaining this function later. Verified the unconverted function still works correctly: clicking a card's bookmark button toggles state.bookmarks via delegation without triggering the card's own detail-open handler, and clicking the card body itself still opens that evidence's detail view.

steps.title: D10 - Q1 — Arrow `this` vs. regular-function `this`
steps.narration: A regular function gets its own this, determined dynamically by how it's called: obj.method() binds it to obj, addEventListener binds it to the listening element, a bare call leaves it undefined in strict mode. An arrow function has no this of its own — it lexically inherits this from whatever scope surrounds it at definition time, and that binding can never be overridden, not even by call/apply/bind. That's exactly why handleEvidenceListClick (T3) has to stay a declaration: it's registered as a DOM handler specifically so the browser can bind this to the listening element, the 'object method' pattern arrow functions break by design. It's preferable for callbacks, like the hypConfidence listener converted in T2, precisely because most callbacks don't want caller-determined this at all — they want to keep meaning whatever this meant in the surrounding code, which arrows give you by default instead of requiring a manual .bind(this).

steps.title: D10 - Q2 — Did the `new`/`arguments` limitations affect any conversion?
steps.narration: No — confirmed by grepping the whole js/ tree for `new <CustomName>(` and for `arguments`: zero hits beyond the built-in new Date()/new Promise()/new Error() calls already in the codebase, and zero uses of the arguments object anywhere — every function here takes named parameters. So neither limitation disqualified any candidate; the real disqualifying factor for handleEvidenceListClick was this-binding (Q1/T3), not arguments or new. The honest answer is that this codebase simply doesn't use either feature.

steps.title: D10 - Q3 — Did hoisting matter anywhere in this refactor?
steps.narration: It mattered enough to check carefully, but didn't block either T1 conversion. Both certaintyBadgeClass and statCardHTML are declared after, textually, the function that calls them (renderTimeline/renderDashboard) — but hoisting only matters for when a reference is actually evaluated, not where a function is textually defined relative to its caller's declaration. renderTimeline's body doesn't run when renderTimeline is declared, only when something later calls renderTimeline() — by which point the whole module's top-level code, including the const line below it, has already finished executing. So the real question is 'is this function ever called before its own const line has run?' — and for both, it isn't. This would matter if a function were called from another function's own top-level module-scope statements before its declaration line ran; neither candidate hit that case.

steps.title: D10 - Q4 — Before/after: behavioral difference or pure style?
steps.narration: Using certaintyBadgeClass as the concrete example (same before/after shown in T1): purely a readability/binding-form change, no runtime difference — verified live by reloading the Timeline view and confirming all 15 rendered badges map exactly as before the conversion. It's purely style here specifically because none of the three things that would make it behavioral apply to this function: it's never called before its own line runs (Q3), it never used this/arguments/new (Q2), and it's module-private either way, so there's no export-binding difference. Same inputs, same outputs, same call sites, same scope — only the syntax changed.

steps.title: D10 - Q5 — Proposed team rule for declarations vs. expressions vs. arrows
steps.narration: Proposed rule, as a single binary test per function: use a named function declaration only if the function is called by something else's this binding (registered directly by reference as a DOM/framework event handler, or ever attached as an object method) or genuinely needs to be callable before its own declaration line runs in the same scope — otherwise, use a const arrow function. In this codebase that keeps handleEvidenceListClick and the other directly-referenced addEventListener targets (renderEvidenceList, clearFilters, renderTimeline as change handlers) as declarations, since they're real or plausible-future DOM-this recipients; everything else — module-private helpers and one-off callbacks — becomes an arrow function. This gives two engineers the same answer without relying on taste, and it's mechanically checkable from a diff: does this function appear as a bare reference in an addEventListener call, or is it invoked before its own declaration executes?

steps.title: Exercise 2 — Build Tooling, TypeScript & CI/CD
steps.narration: Section marker: everything from here on is Exercise 2 — moving Project ReMotion from a plain <script> tag to npm + Vite + TypeScript, with GitHub Actions running lint/format and deploying to GitHub Pages on every push to main.

steps.title: D1 - T1 — Chose npm over pnpm
steps.narration: npm ships with Node itself, so no extra global install is needed on a single-laptop coursework repo — pnpm's real advantage (a shared content-addressable store across many projects, saving disk/install time) doesn't pay off here since this is the only project using this toolchain on this machine. Recorded as package.json's own devDependencies plus package-lock.json.

steps.title: D1 - T2 — package.json initialized with real metadata
steps.narration: npm init -y scaffolded it, then filled in description, type: module, author, license and repo links by hand — npm's auto-guess left generic placeholders (author: "", license: "ISC") that wouldn't mean anything for this repo.

steps.title: D1 - T3 — .gitignore covers node_modules/, dist/, *.tsbuildinfo
steps.narration: node_modules/ is fully reinstallable from package-lock.json so it never belongs in git; dist/ (Demo 3) and *.tsbuildinfo (Demo 5) are build output added ahead of time so later demos don't need a second .gitignore commit.

steps.title: D1 - T4 — Vite installed, package-lock.json committed
steps.narration: npm install --save-dev vite added the first real dependency and generated package-lock.json, committed alongside package.json in the same commit (0d69109) so CI and any other machine resolve the exact same dependency tree, not just a compatible one.

steps.title: D1 - Q1 — What a package manager solves that manual download doesn't
steps.narration: Manually downloading a library means manually tracking its own dependencies (and their versions), re-doing that by hand every time a version changes, and having no single source of truth for what's actually installed. npm resolves the full dependency graph (Vite alone pulls in ~15 packages transitively), dedupes shared sub-dependencies, and records the exact resolved tree in package-lock.json — none of which "put it in a folder yourself" gives you.

steps.title: D1 - Q2 — dependencies vs devDependencies
steps.narration: dependencies ship inside the built app the user's browser actually runs; devDependencies are only needed while building/testing/linting on a developer's or CI machine. Vite, ESLint, Prettier and TypeScript are all devDependencies here — none of their code ends up in dist/, they only transform/check the source before it gets there. This app currently has zero runtime dependencies (no framework), so the dependencies field stays empty.

steps.title: D1 - Q3 — What a lockfile is for
steps.narration: A lockfile pins the exact resolved version (and sub-dependency versions) of everything installed, not just the semver ranges in package.json. Without it committed, a teammate (or CI) running npm install later could resolve a newer transitive version that behaves differently — works on my machine, breaks in CI is exactly the failure mode a missing lockfile invites.

steps.title: D1 - Q4 — What npm gives up vs pnpm on a larger project
steps.narration: pnpm keeps one global content-addressable store on disk and hard-links packages into each project's node_modules, so ten projects using the same Vite version store it once, not ten times, and installs are faster since most packages are already on disk. npm duplicates full copies per project. On a single small repo like this one the difference is negligible; on a machine running many Node projects (like this one, per Developer/CLAUDE.md's project list) it would add up — a legitimate reason to reconsider pnpm later, just not the deciding factor here.

steps.title: D2 - T1 — Vite installed and configured
steps.narration: data/ and assets/ moved into public/ (Vite only copies public/ contents verbatim into dist/ on build — see Demo 3); index.html and js/ needed no restructuring since Exercise 1's ES-module split already put them where Vite expects. vite.config.js sets base: "./" for the GitHub Pages subpath deploy in Demo 9.

steps.title: D2 - T2 — Dev server verified functionally identical
steps.narration: Not just "it loads": curled every static path (/, /js/main.js, /data/case.json, /assets/logo/logo.svg) for 200s, then drove the real app through a browser across all 5 views — 18 evidence cards, 6 people cards with images actually loading, 15 timeline events, the workspace hypothesis form's populated selects — identical counts to the pre-Vite static-server version.

steps.title: D2 - T3 — Real HMR observed
steps.narration: Edited .app-header's background color in styles.css while the app was mid-session on #workspace. Vite's log showed "hmr update /styles.css"; the new color applied instantly, and a JS marker set on window plus the URL hash both survived — proof it was a hot style swap, not a full page reload. Reverted immediately after (net diff on styles.css: zero).

steps.after: background: #d1495b; /* HMR test — reverted right after */

steps.title: D2 - Q1 — Vite dev server vs a plain static file server
steps.narration: A plain static server (python -m http.server, Exercise 1) just serves files byte-for-byte off disk. Vite's dev server additionally transforms each file on the fly per-request (TypeScript stripped, later demos), serves an injected client script that opens a WebSocket back to the server for live updates, and knows the module graph well enough to only re-send what actually changed — none of which a bytes-off-disk server can do.

steps.title: D2 - Q2 — What HMR is and what was (and wasn't) observed
steps.narration: Hot Module Replacement swaps a changed module's code into the already-running page over the existing WebSocket, without reloading the page. Observed: the new CSS applied live. Not observed (deliberately, since it didn't happen): the page did NOT reload — confirmed because a window-scoped JS variable I set beforehand was still there afterward, and the URL hash stayed on #workspace instead of resetting to #dashboard the way a full reload would.

steps.title: D2 - Q3 — Why ES modules integrate naturally with Vite
steps.narration: Vite's dev server IS an ES-module server at its core — it serves each imported file as its own module and resolves import/export statements natively in the browser, which only works if the source is already written as real import/export in the first place. The pre-Exercise-1 single <script> version had no module graph for Vite to serve at all; it would have needed bundling just to run under Vite's dev server, defeating the point of an unbundled dev server.

steps.title: D3 - T1 — vite build inspected
steps.narration: npm run build produced dist/index.html, dist/assets/index-*.{js,css} (hashed, minified, bundled from all 16 source modules into one file each), and dist/data/*.json + dist/assets/** copied verbatim from public/ — confirming public/ was the right place for Demo 2's file move.

steps.title: D3 - T2 — vite preview served the actual built output
steps.narration: Ran npm run preview (not the dev server) on port 4173 and drove the built app through all 5 views with the same checks as Demo 2's dev-server pass — 18/6/15/18 counts across evidence/people/timeline/workspace, identical to every other verification in this exercise.

steps.title: D3 - T3 — Dev source vs. built output compared
steps.narration: js/main.js in dev: 95 lines, one file, no minification. The production bundle: all 16 modules concatenated into one ~24KB file with zero newlines (single line), shortened via esbuild's minifier, plus Vite's own modulepreload polyfill prepended — a concrete, measured before/after, not an assumption.

steps.title: D3 - Q1 — Three transformations actually observed
steps.narration: 1) Bundling — 16 separate ES modules became one JS file. 2) Minification — whitespace/newlines stripped, the whole bundle collapsed to a single line. 3) Hashed filenames — index-Dw0W39qB.js instead of main.js, a new hash every time the content changes (confirmed: the hash changed across three separate builds in this session as the source changed).

steps.title: D3 - Q2 — Why production filenames get a content hash
steps.narration: It lets a CDN/browser cache these files essentially forever (immutable, max-age far in the future) while still guaranteeing a user always gets the latest version after a deploy: the filename itself changes when the content does, so there's never a stale-cache-vs-fresh-deploy conflict to invalidate by hand.

steps.title: D3 - Q3 — Why the dev server itself should never go to real users
steps.narration: It ships every module unbundled and unminified (far more HTTP requests, much larger total payload), it has zero built-in cache-busting story, and it runs a WebSocket-based dev-only protocol (the HMR client from Demo 2) with no production hardening — it's optimized entirely for edit-save-see-the-change speed, not for serving real traffic.

steps.title: D4 - T1 — ESLint (flat config) + Prettier installed
steps.narration: eslint.config.js uses @eslint/js's recommended rules plus eslint-config-prettier last in the array so Prettier's own formatting opinions always win over ESLint's stylistic ones. Scoped away from the vendored create-presentation skill engine and generated dist/ — those aren't the app being migrated.

steps.title: D4 - T2 — lint / lint:fix / format / format:check scripts
steps.narration: All four do something real: lint runs eslint . (0 errors after fixes below), lint:fix adds --fix, format runs prettier --write . scoped to app source, format:check runs prettier --check for CI (wired into Demo 8's workflow).

steps.title: D4 - Q1 — Linter checks vs formatter checks
steps.narration: A linter checks code correctness/patterns (unused variables, ==  vs ===, var vs let/const) — things that can hide real bugs. A formatter only checks/fixes whitespace, quote style, line wrapping — purely cosmetic, never behavior-affecting. Concrete finding from each: ESLint caught the real unused resolvedTerm bug above; Prettier rewrapped a long boolean expression across lines in lookup.js's formatDate with no behavior change at all.

steps.title: D4 - Q2 — Why lint and lint:fix are separate scripts
steps.narration: Auto-fixing every finding is only safe for purely mechanical issues (spacing, quote style); a real bug like the unused resolvedTerm needs a human to decide what the right fix actually is — ESLint can't know whether an unused value should be deleted, renamed, or is a sign of a missing line of logic. CI (Demo 8) deliberately runs the non-fixing lint, so a finding fails the build loudly instead of being silently auto-corrected in a place no one will ever review the diff.

steps.title: D4 - Q3 — What npm run lint does under the hood
steps.narration: npm looks up "lint" in package.json's scripts, then resolves the bare `eslint` command by checking node_modules/.bin/ first (where npm installs a symlink for every installed package's CLI) before falling back to the system PATH. Since eslint is a devDependency here, node_modules/.bin/eslint always exists after npm install — it would work the same on any machine that ran npm install, and would silently use a different (or missing) global eslint if it weren't a project dependency at all.

Downgraded TypeScript from 7.x to 6.0.3 for typescript-eslint compatibility (its peer range caps at <6.1.0).

steps.title: D5 - T2 — lookup.ts, storage.ts, navigation.ts converted, zero any
steps.narration: The three smallest/most clearly-utility modules — formatting/lookup helpers, localStorage read/write, hash routing. Where a function touched state.js's still-untyped exports, committed to the narrowest real shape needed (an Identifiable{id:string} for the finder functions) rather than accepting the any that would otherwise leak in.

steps.title: D5 - T3 — tsc wired into build, proven to actually block
steps.narration: package.json's build script became "npm run typecheck && vite build". Verified for real: broke formatDate()'s return type on purpose, confirmed npm run build failed at the typecheck step before vite build ever ran, then reverted and confirmed it passes again.

"build": "npm run typecheck && vite build",

steps.title: D5 - Q1 — What strict actually turns on
steps.narration: strict bundles several independent checks — strictNullChecks (null/undefined must be handled explicitly, not silently assignable to everything) and noImplicitAny (every value needs an inferable or declared type, not a silent any) are the two that mattered most here. Kept both on: they're exactly what would have caught Exercise 1's undefined-access and implicit-any bugs at compile time instead of runtime.

steps.title: D5 - Q2 — Compile-time errors vs Exercise 1's runtime bugs
steps.narration: A compile-time type error is caught before the code ever runs, by static analysis of the declared shapes; Exercise 1's bugs (a stale var closure, a dropped await, a shared array reference) were all caught by actually running the code and observing wrong behavior. TypeScript alone would NOT have caught most of them — a stale closure and a shared array reference are both perfectly type-correct, wrong only in runtime timing/aliasing, which types don't model. It likely would have caught the dropped-await bug, since an un-awaited async call used where a value was expected produces a Promise<T> vs T mismatch.

steps.title: D5 - Q3 — What any does, and why avoid it even though it's faster
steps.narration: any opts a value out of type checking entirely — every property access, call, and assignment on it is accepted with zero verification, and that unchecked-ness silently spreads to anything the any value touches. Reaching for it would have been faster in the moment, but it would have made this exact TS setup unable to catch the bugs it exists to catch — an any-typed state.js export flowing into lookup.ts would make every one of its consumers unchecked too.

steps.title: D6 - T1 — Person/Location/Evidence/TimelineEvent/CaseInfo typed
steps.narration: Verified against every record in public/data/*.json via a one-off Python pass, not just the first item. Evidence.status/.relevance are closed literal unions (the app branches on them); Evidence.type stays a plain string since nothing branches on it and the real data already has a case-varying outlier ("Test-Report" vs "test-report").
steps.after:
export type EvidenceStatus = "unreviewed" | "reviewed" | "flagged";
export type EvidenceRelevance = "unknown" | "relevant" | "irrelevant";

steps.title: D6 - T2 — dataLoading.ts casts every fetch boundary
steps.narration: state.ts declares every collection with its real type; dataLoading.ts casts each fetch()/.json() result `as <Type>` right at the network boundary, replacing the Identifiable/BookmarkId/NotesStore stand-ins Demo 5 needed while state.js was still untyped.
steps.after:
const peopleRes = await fetch("data/people.json");
state.allPeople = (await peopleRes.json()) as Person[];

steps.title: D6 - T3 — personIds' id-vs-name ambiguity, resolved by normalizing
steps.narration: public/data/evidence.json's personIds is meant to hold Person ids, but E04 actually holds "Nova Byte" — a display name — instead of "nova-byte" (found by cross-checking every personIds entry against people.json's real ids). Typing personIds as PersonId[] forced a real choice: keep the type loose enough to admit id-or-name, or normalize once at the load boundary. Chose to normalize — dataLoading.ts's normalizePersonIds runs right after both evidence and people load — so evidenceMentionsPerson no longer needs to know Person has a name field at all.

steps.title: D6 - Q1 — How the JS version got away without deciding
steps.narration: Plain JS never declares what personIds "is" anywhere — it's just an array of strings, and .indexOf() doesn't care whether the string is an id or a name. The original code even had a defensive dual-match (check both person.id and person.name) baked into evidenceMentionsPerson, quietly working around the inconsistency instead of fixing it. Typing personIds as PersonId[] made that ambiguity visible and forced an explicit decision — normalize at load time — instead of leaving the workaround in place forever.

steps.title: D6 - Q2 — What static types can't catch: bad JSON content
steps.narration: Yes — evidence.json has one record with "Reviewed" (capitalized) instead of "reviewed" and one "Unknown" instead of "unknown", values the EvidenceStatus/EvidenceRelevance unions say can't happen. The `as Evidence[]` cast in dataLoading.ts doesn't validate anything at runtime, so both sail straight through unnoticed — only getStatusBadgeClass/getRelevanceBadgeClass's pre-existing .toLowerCase() (from Exercise 1) is what actually prevents this from breaking visibly. Catching this for real needs runtime validation (e.g. a schema check on the parsed JSON, like zod), which is outside what static types alone do.

steps.title: D6 - Q3 — interface vs type alias for the domain models
steps.narration: Used interface for the four object-shaped domain entities (Person, Location, Evidence, TimelineEvent, CaseInfo) and type for everything else (the union/literal types like EvidenceStatus, and the PersonId/LocationId string aliases). For these specific closed, never-intersected shapes it doesn't materially matter — interface just reads as the more conventional choice for "this is a named domain entity," and type is the only option anyway for a union like EvidenceStatus, which can't be expressed as an interface at all.

steps.title: D7 - T1 — Every remaining .js converted, zero TS errors
steps.narration: main.ts and all five view modules converted; tsconfig's allowJs/checkJs bridge removed since there's nothing left to bridge to. Compiles clean under the same strict settings from Demo 5. Added js/dom.ts's el<T>(id) helper — one small wrapper instead of scattering `as HTMLSelectElement` casts across five files, which stopped being premature by the third file needing the same pattern (rule of three).

steps.title: D7 - T2 — Three real compiler-forced decisions
steps.narration: 1) state.ts's caseData modeled as CaseInfo | null (not CaseInfo | {}) since case.json genuinely hasn't loaded yet during init — confirmed load-bearing by reverting one `?.` and getting a real TS18047 error. 2) Evidence needed a bookmarked?:boolean field it never had — not in JSON at all, only set at runtime; missing it was a real compile error, not a nit. 3) timeline.ts's reused `let modal` across an if-branch stayed "possibly null" to TS even though it never is at runtime — rewritten as one `existingModal ?? document.createElement(...)` binding, clearer code too.

steps.title: D7 - T3 — Behavior confirmed identical, not assumed
steps.narration: Full Playwright pass against both the dev server and a fresh production build: evidence card open/close, status/relevance selects mutating the loaded record, note save + preview, bookmark toggle propagating to the Workspace list, hypothesis form save-and-reload round-trip through localStorage, timeline quick-view modal, people/locations tab switch — every count and behavior matches every prior demo's baseline.

steps.title: D7 - Q1 — A type error that took real thought
steps.narration: timeline.ts's openEvidenceModal (see T2 above): the compiler wasn't wrong that `modal` was "possibly null" after the if-branch reassignment — it genuinely couldn't prove the invariant that isNewModal-false implies non-null, because that invariant lives in two separate variables' correlated history, not in either one's type. Plain JS/manual review had already "verified" this code worked (it does) without ever noticing the implicit coupling; TS forced making that coupling structural instead of implicit.

steps.title: D7 - Q2 — When any is the right call during a migration
steps.narration: Never reached for it in this migration — every real gap (untyped upstream data, DOM element casts, JSON parse results) had a narrower honest answer available (unknown + a cast, a local minimal interface, a generic helper). The line: any is defensible only as a last-resort escape hatch for something genuinely un-typeable in the time available, always with a comment explaining why and ideally a tracking note to revisit it — not a default reach whenever a real type would take a few extra minutes to think through.

steps.title: D7 - Q3 — Did the migration reveal a genuine bug?
steps.narration: The clearest case is the personIds id-vs-name inconsistency (Demo 6): the pre-migration JS worked around it silently with a dual id-or-name match instead of ever surfacing it as a data problem. That's a genuine, previously-unnoticed data-quality issue, not noise — it was invisible in JS precisely because nothing forced the code to commit to what personIds actually contains. The three Demo 7 spots (T2 above) are closer to "noise" in the sense that none of them changed behavior — they made already-correct assumptions explicit rather than catching an actual bug.

steps.title: D8 - T1 — .github/workflows/dev.yml
steps.narration: Triggers on push and pull_request, checks out, sets up Node 24 with actions/setup-node's built-in npm cache (keyed off package-lock.json), npm ci, then npm run lint and npm run format:check.

steps.title: D8 - T2 — Pushed a real lint break, watched it fail
steps.narration: Commit b2bad25 added a genuinely unused local variable to lookup.ts. Confirmed via the public Actions API: run 36332660056 completed with conclusion "failure" — not assumed from reading the YAML, actually observed on GitHub.

steps.title: D8 - T3 — Reverted, watched it pass again
steps.narration: Commit ac85ca9 removed the unused variable; run 36332697148 completed with conclusion "success" — a real fail-then-pass pair on the same workflow, both confirmed via the Actions API rather than eyeballed once and assumed stable.

steps.title: D8 - Q1 — Workflow, job, and step in dev.yml
steps.narration: The workflow is the whole dev.yml file (name: "Dev checks"). It has one job, lint-and-format, which runs on ubuntu-latest. That job has six steps, e.g. "Set up Node.js" (actions/setup-node@v4) and "Lint" (run: npm run lint) — a step is one action or shell command inside a job.

steps.title: D8 - Q2 — Why run lint in CI if it already runs locally
steps.narration: Because "could run locally" isn't "did run locally" — nothing stops a commit from being pushed without anyone having run npm run lint first, especially under time pressure. CI is the one place every single push is checked the same way regardless of what any individual developer remembered to do, which is exactly what caught this exercise's real b2bad25 lint break.

steps.title: D8 - Q3 — What dependency caching does here
steps.narration: actions/setup-node's cache: "npm" caches ~/.npm keyed on a hash of package-lock.json, so a run with an unchanged lockfile restores the download cache instead of re-fetching every package from the registry. Removing it wouldn't break correctness (npm ci still installs the exact locked versions either way) — it would just make every single run slower, re-downloading the same ~15 packages from scratch every time.

steps.title: D9 - T1 — .github/workflows/deploy.yml
steps.narration: On push to main: checkout, install, lint, npm run build (tsc typecheck + vite build), upload dist/ as a Pages artifact, then a separate deploy job publishes it via actions/deploy-pages. permissions: contents: read, pages: write, id-token: write.
steps.after:
permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write

steps.title: D9 - T2 — Live URL confirmed serving the app end-to-end
steps.narration: Benjamin enabled GitHub Pages (source: GitHub Actions) in repo settings, unblocking this. Live at https://bennilic.github.io/mystery-road-awe-2026/ — visited directly with a browser (not assumed from a green Actions run) and confirmed all 5 views render with the same data counts as every local verification all through this exercise: 18 evidence cards, 6 people cards with images actually loading from the deployed assets/ path, 15 timeline events, 18 hypothesis-evidence options, zero console errors.

steps.title: D9 - T3 — A real change, pushed, live with no manual step
steps.narration: Pushed commit 2e3316a straight to main: a real favicon fix (every Playwright pass in this whole exercise had logged a genuine favicon.ico 404 — <link rel="icon"> now points at the existing logo.svg). Confirmed via the Actions jobs/steps API — not assumed — that run 36397494889's build job passed and its deploy job actually succeeded this time (previously it failed only at the "Deploy to GitHub Pages" step; now that step is green too). The fix is live at the URL above with zero manual deployment step — <link rel="icon"> is present in the served HTML.

steps.title: D9 - Q1 — Why deploy.yml re-runs lint and build itself
steps.narration: "It already passed on my machine" (or even in Demo 8's separate workflow run) says nothing about what's actually on main at the moment deploy.yml runs — a different commit could be on main than what dev.yml last checked, or dev.yml could have been skipped entirely for that push. The only way to guarantee what gets deployed is exactly what was verified is to lint and build the exact commit being deployed, in the same job that deploys it.

steps.title: D9 - Q2 — The actual publish mechanism
steps.narration: actions/upload-pages-artifact packages dist/ as a build artifact tied to this specific workflow run; actions/deploy-pages then takes that artifact and publishes it to the repo's GitHub Pages environment via GitHub's own deployment API, authenticated with a short-lived OIDC token minted from the id-token: write permission — not a push to a gh-pages branch, and not a personal access token stored as a secret.

steps.title: D9 - Q3 — What changes for a different static host
steps.narration: The build job (checkout, install, lint, npm run build) would stay exactly the same — dist/ is a plain static site regardless of where it's served. What changes is only the publish step: actions/upload-pages-artifact + actions/deploy-pages would be replaced with, e.g., Netlify's/Vercel's own deploy action (needing an API token stored as a repo secret) or an SFTP/rsync step (needing host/credentials secrets) — and the pages: write/id-token: write permissions would no longer be needed since those are GitHub-Pages-specific.

steps.title: D10 - T1 — Deliberate TS error blocks before the deploy step
steps.narration: Changed formatDate()'s return type to number while its body still returned strings. Confirmed via the Actions API job/step breakdown: build job failed specifically at the "Build" step (tsc), the "Upload... artifact" step shows skipped, and the deploy job's own status is skipped — it never even started, let alone reached the actual Pages publish step. Reverted and confirmed a clean run afterward.
steps.before: export function formatDate(ts: string | number | null | undefined): string {
steps.after: export function formatDate(ts: string | number | null | undefined): number { // deliberate break — reverted

steps.title: D10 - T2 — Exact permissions identified and located
steps.narration: deploy.yml's permissions: block: contents: read (checkout), pages: write and id-token: write (both required by actions/deploy-pages — neither is in GITHUB_TOKEN's default grant, both had to be listed explicitly). No secrets at all — deploy-pages authenticates via a short-lived OIDC token from id-token: write, not a stored PAT.

steps.title: D10 - T3 — Run history read and explained via the Actions API
steps.narration: Walked the job/step breakdown for multiple runs across this session: a clean pass (build+deploy both succeed except the Pages-not-enabled blocker), a lint failure (dev.yml, b2bad25), and a typecheck failure that skips deploy entirely (397949d). Each one's exact failing step was identified from the API's per-step status/conclusion fields, not guessed from the overall red/green.

steps.title: D10 - Q1 — What happens to the live app when build fails
steps.narration: The previously-deployed version stays live — actions/deploy-pages only publishes a new deployment when the workflow actually reaches that step; a failed build job never produces an artifact for it to publish, so there's nothing to replace the current deployment with. This is exactly the behavior wanted: a broken build should never be able to take down or corrupt a working live site.

steps.title: D10 - Q2 — Permissions/secrets needed, and over-granting risk
steps.narration: pages: write and id-token: write, granted via deploy.yml's own permissions: block (repo Settings → Actions → General also has a repo-wide default that this workflow-level block overrides down to only what it needs). No stored secrets. The risk of over-granting (e.g. leaving the repo-wide default at read/write for everything) is that ANY workflow in the repo — including one an attacker adds via a malicious PR — would inherit broad push/write access, not just this one trusted deploy workflow.

steps.title: D10 - Q3 — push vs pull_request vs workflow_dispatch
steps.narration: on: push runs automatically whenever new commits land on the matching ref — used for both workflows here, since both should react automatically to real changes. on: pull_request runs for PR activity specifically (also on dev.yml, so a PR gets checked before it's even merged). on: workflow_dispatch is a manual, human-triggered button in the Actions UI — used for neither workflow here, since both should be fully automatic; it would make sense for something like an on-demand redeploy with no code change.
